issues.legal_issue: A tenancy interest preserved upon repeal remains subject to the later application of the replacement tenancy statute when an amendment brings the land within that statute.
material_facts: The agricultural land was within two miles of a municipal borough, so the 1948 Act originally excluded it under section 88(1)(c).
The lease was extended under the 1939 Act, as amended in 1946, and the lessee’s acquired interest was preserved when the 1948 Act repealed the 1939 Act.
The 1952 amendment brought the land within the 1948 Act while the preserved lease was still subsisting and the eviction suit was pending.
issues.conclusion: The landlord could not evict the tenants except in the manner prescribed by the 1948 Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 89(2)(b)(i) of the 1948 Act preserves rights acquired before the Act commenced. Section 88(1)(c), which excluded specified areas from the Act, does not negate that saving: as held in Sakharam alias Bapusaheb Narayan Sanas v. Manikchand Motichand Shah, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 59, the exclusion is prospective and not confiscatory, and a legally recognized right has a remedy through the general law where no special forum is provided. After the 1952 amendment brought the land within the 1948 Act, termination of the subsisting tenancy had to follow section 14.

predicates.protected_tenancy_interest_survived_repe: The tenant had acquired a legally recognized tenancy interest under an earlier law, and that interest survived the law’s repeal.
predicates.land_was_later_brought_within_tenancy_ac: A later change brought the land within the scope of a tenancy-protection law.
predicates.protected_lease_remained_in_force_at_ext: The tenancy interest preserved under the earlier law was still in force when the later change took effect.
predicates.eviction_suit_pending: A court was considering a proceeding seeking eviction of the tenant.

issues.definition: When a protected tenancy interest survives repeal and remains in force when the land later comes within a tenancy-protection law, an eviction proceeding must comply with that law.

issues.legal_issue: A termination notice cannot support eviction when the tenancy has been statutorily extended beyond the date on which the notice purports to end it.
material_facts: The lease was originally granted for six years, but the 1939 Act, as amended in 1946, extended it to a minimum of ten years after that Act applied to the land.
The landlord gave notice purporting to terminate the lease before the statutorily extended term expired and filed an eviction suit on the basis of that notice.
The tenancy had also come within the 1948 Act before the suit was disposed of.
issues.conclusion: The notice had become ineffective, so the landlord could obtain no relief on its basis and there was no need to remand the case to decide the other issues raised in the suit; the landlord could pursue any appropriate proceeding allowed by law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(1)(b) of the 1939 Act, as amended in 1946, deemed a subsisting lease to be for a period of not less than ten years. A notice that purported to end the tenancy before the end of that statutorily extended term could not support eviction. Because the pending eviction claim rested on that ineffective notice, the unresolved issues did not require remand in that suit.

predicates.eviction_suit_pending: A court was considering a proceeding seeking eviction of the tenant.
predicates.eviction_claim_relied_on_termination_not: The landlord relied on a notice purporting to terminate the tenancy as the basis for eviction.
predicates.notice_set_end_before_statutorily_extend: The notice purported to end the tenancy before the end of a term extended by law.

issues.definition: In an eviction suit based on a termination notice, if the notice sets an end date earlier than the end of the tenancy’s statutory extension, the notice cannot support eviction.
